| A parameter table for `tunnel()`, `BoxTunnel`, or `SocketAddress` | [How tunnels work](/cloud/tunnels#parameters-and-returns) |


# Control inbound and outbound access to a box
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/network-policy

Decide who may reach a Cloud box — keep it private, share one port through a signed link, or make it public — and set what the box itself is allowed to reach on the way out.

Two questions decide a box's network posture: who is allowed to reach it, and what it is allowed to reach. The inbound half is the public flag and preview URLs; the outbound half is `NetworkSpec`. Dialing a box port from your own code is a different job, and [Network](/cloud/network) covers it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The routes on this page live under `/api/box/...` — the **platform API**, which is a separate surface from the SDK REST API at `/v1/boxes/...` used everywhere else in these docs. The singular `box` and the missing version segment are intentional, not typos.

## Prerequisites

* An API key exported as `BOXLITE_API_KEY`, and the base URL as `BOXLITE_REST_URL`. See [API keys](/cloud/api-keys).
* A running box with a service listening on a TCP port, bound to `0.0.0.0`.
* Write access to boxes in your organization, for the public flag.

## Inbound: who can reach a box

A box is private or public, and any single port on it can be shared through a preview URL. Those are two independent decisions: the flag governs the box, the URL governs one port.

### A new box is private

Inbound access is **disabled unless you ask for it**. Create a box without saying
anything about inbound and nothing outside it can reach its services — which is the
posture you want for almost every box, and the reason you rarely need the public flag
at all.

Ask for the other posture at creation time with `inbound`:

```python Python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
from boxlite import BoxOptions, InboundNetworkSpec, NetworkSpec

opts = BoxOptions(
    image="python",
    network=NetworkSpec(inbound=InboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled")),
)
```

```bash CLI theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
boxlite create --image python --inbound enabled
```

`mode` takes `"enabled"` or `"disabled"`, and `"disabled"` is what you get by omission.
Writing it out explicitly sends the same request as leaving it off — it documents the
intent for the next reader, nothing more.

| What you create the box with | How Cloud records it |
| - | - |
| no `network` field | private |
| `NetworkSpec()` | private |
| `inbound=InboundNetworkSpec(mode="disabled")` | private |
| `inbound=InboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled")` | **public** |
| `NetworkSpec(mode="enabled")` — the flat form | private |

> [!NOTE]
>
> The SDK does not read this back: `BoxInfo.network` is `None` on Cloud, so you cannot
> check a box's inbound posture from `await box.info()`. Read it from the box's row in
> the console instead.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **This default changed in 0.10.5, and the old spelling for "public" no longer means
> that.** `NetworkSpec` used to take a flat `mode` and `allow_net`; those now configure
> **outbound only**. Code that said:
>
> ```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> network=NetworkSpec(mode="enabled")       # outbound — never makes the box public
> ```
>
> produced a public box before 0.10.5 and produces a **private** one now, so a tunnel
> against it fails:
>
> ```
> Box ${boxId} is not public; set public: true before opening a tunnel
> ```
>
> Add the inbound half:
>
> ```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> from boxlite import InboundNetworkSpec, NetworkSpec, OutboundNetworkSpec
>
> network=NetworkSpec(
>     inbound=InboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled"),
>     outbound=OutboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled"),
> )
> ```

`InboundNetworkSpec` carries an `allow_net` field for symmetry with the outbound side,
but no layer enforces an inbound allowlist, so a non-empty value is refused before the
request leaves your process:

```
InvalidArgumentError: invalid argument: inbound.allow_net is not supported yet; remove it (inbound access is controlled by mode only)
```

Inbound is governed by `mode` alone. To let one audience in rather than everyone, keep
the box private and share a [signed URL](#share-a-port-temporarily-with-a-signed-url).

You are not locked in: the public flag below flips an existing box either way, without
recreating it or losing its filesystem.

### Where to do each of these

Most of this section is shown as HTTP because that is the only surface some of it
has. Two of the four operations are also in the console, and those are the ones you
will reach for by hand:

| Operation | Console | SDK / CLI | HTTP |
| - | - | - | - |
| Set inbound when you create a box | — | **Yes** — `inbound`, or `--inbound` | Yes |
| Change inbound on an existing box | **Yes** — the box's **network** panel | No | Yes |
| Get a preview URL for a port | **Yes** — **get url** on the same panel | No | Yes |
| Issue an expiring signed URL | No | No | **Only here** |
| Revoke a signed URL | No | No | **Only here** |

The SDK's network handle exposes `tunnel(port)` and nothing else, and `boxlite
network` has only `tunnel`, so neither can change inbound or mint a preview URL.
Reach for HTTP when you are automating; reach for the console when you are not.

### A preview URL and an SDK tunnel are different tools

A preview URL is an HTTPS address for one port on one box, served by BoxLite's preview proxy. Anything that speaks HTTPS can fetch it — a browser, `curl`, a webhook sender, a reviewer on their phone — and none of them needs the BoxLite SDK.

An SDK tunnel is the other shape. Your code asks the box for a tunnel and dials it with your API key, and the tunnel carries any TCP protocol rather than only HTTP.

Reach for a **preview URL** when something outside your own code has to fetch an HTTP service in the box: a browser preview, a webhook receiver, a link you send someone. Reach for a **tunnel** when your program is the client, or when the protocol is not HTTP — SSH, a database wire protocol, a raw byte stream. Tunnels are documented on [Network](/cloud/network).

### Make a box public or private

> [tab] Console
>
> Open the box, find the **network** panel, and use the **Inbound access** switch.
>
> The panel states the current posture in the terms that matter:
>
> | It reads | What it means |
> | - | - |
> | `inbound · disabled · your organization` | A preview URL sends an unknown visitor through sign-in, and serves only members of your organization |
> | `inbound · enabled · anyone` | A preview URL serves anyone who holds it, with no sign-in |
>
> Turning it on asks you to confirm — *"Open this box's preview URLs to anyone?"* —
> because that is exactly what it does. **`outbound` on the same panel is read-only:**
> nothing changes a box's egress after it is created.

> [tab] HTTP
>
> ```http theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> POST /api/box/{boxIdOrName}/public/{isPublic}
> ```
>
> Both values travel in the path. There is no request body, and a `200` returns the box.
>
> | Path parameter | Type | Required | Description |
> | - | - | - | - |
> | `boxIdOrName` | string | Required | The box id, or the name you gave the box when you created it |
> | `isPublic` | boolean | Required | `true` opens the box to unauthenticated access, `false` returns it to private |
>
> The call needs write access to boxes in your organization, and it is recorded in your organization's audit trail.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
# Make a box public. Read the key from the environment -- never inline it.
BOXLITE_REST_URL="${BOXLITE_REST_URL:-https://api.boxlite.ai}"

curl -fsS -X POST \
  "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/box/review-app-142/public/true" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${BOXLITE_API_KEY}"
```

Be clear-eyed about what you just did. **A public box drops the credential requirement in front of it: anyone who has a URL to it can reach the service, from anywhere, with no API key and no token, and that holds until you set the flag back to `false`.** A URL is a string — it travels in chat messages, tickets, browser history, referrer headers, and screenshots. Anything the service in that box can read or write is now guarded by the secrecy of a link, so treat the box's files, its environment variables, and its network credentials as exposed for as long as the flag is on. Set it back to private the moment you no longer need it:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
BOXLITE_REST_URL="${BOXLITE_REST_URL:-https://api.boxlite.ai}"

curl -fsS -X POST \
  "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/box/review-app-142/public/false" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${BOXLITE_API_KEY}"
```

If what you actually want is to let one person see one port for a short while, do not touch this flag at all — use a signed preview URL instead.

### Get a preview URL for a port

> [tab] Console
>
> On the box's **network** panel, choose **get url** and type the port.
>
> > [!NOTE]
> >
> > **That button is disabled while inbound is disabled.** The HTTP route is not — it
> > returns a URL and a token for a private box too, which is what the token flow below
> > is for. If **get url** is greyed out and you expected otherwise, the box is private,
> > not broken.

> [tab] HTTP
>
> ```http theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> GET /api/box/{boxIdOrName}/ports/{port}/preview-url
> ```
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> BOXLITE_REST_URL="${BOXLITE_REST_URL:-https://api.boxlite.ai}"
>
> curl -fsS \
>   "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/box/review-app-142/ports/8080/preview-url" \
>   -H "Authorization: Bearer ${BOXLITE_API_KEY}" | jq
> ```
>
> A `200` returns:
>
> | Field | Type | Description |
> | - | - | - |
> | `boxId` | string | The box the URL points at |
> | `url` | string | The preview address, shaped `https://{port}-{encodedBoxId}.{proxyDomain}` |
> | `token` | string | The access token for that URL |

The port is part of the URL, so **a preview URL addresses one port, not the whole box.** A box running an app on `8080` and a metrics endpoint on `9090` has two preview URLs, and you fetch each one separately. Change the port your service listens on and the old URL no longer describes it.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Holding the URL is not enough — a tunnel has to be open on that port.** The endpoint
> hands you a URL for any port you name, including one nothing is listening on. The proxy
> then checks, on every request, that the port has a live tunnel, and answers `404`
> when it does not:
>
> ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> {"statusCode":404,"message":"not found: tunnel not found","code":"NOT_FOUND"}
> ```
>
> A `404` here is therefore about the *tunnel*, not about your path. Open one for each
> port you intend to expose — `box.network.tunnel(<PORT>)` in the SDK — and a port
> without one stays unreachable no matter how well-formed its URL looks.

#### Present the token when the box is private

A private box's preview URL is not open, so a request has to carry the `token` from the response above. The preview proxy accepts it three ways, and tries them in this order:

| How | Form | Use it for |
| - | - | - |
| `Authorization` header | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | A programmatic client you control |
| Dedicated header | `X-BoxLite-Preview-Token: <token>` | A client that already uses `Authorization` for something else |
| Query parameter | `?BOXLITE_BOX_AUTH_KEY=<token>` | A browser, or any client that can only follow a URL |

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
# A private preview URL, fetched with the token in a header
curl -fsS "https://8080-<ENCODED_BOX_ID>.<PROXY_DOMAIN>/health" \
  -H "X-BoxLite-Preview-Token: ${BOXLITE_PREVIEW_TOKEN}"
```

The query-parameter form is what makes a private preview URL openable in a browser: append it once, and the proxy strips the parameter before the request reaches your service, then sets a cookie so the following requests on that host carry the authorization for you. Because that form puts a credential in a URL, treat such a link like a password — it lands in browser history, server logs, and anything the recipient pastes it into. For sharing with a person, a [signed URL](#share-a-port-temporarily-with-a-signed-url) is the better instrument: it expires on its own and you can revoke it.

A request that carries no credential the proxy accepts is redirected to sign in, so a human reaching a private box in a browser can authenticate instead of being refused outright.

### Share a port temporarily with a signed URL

> [!NOTE]
>
> Signed URLs are **HTTP-only**. There is no console control and no SDK or CLI method
> for issuing or revoking one, so the calls below are the whole of it.

```http theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
GET /api/box/{boxIdOrName}/ports/{port}/signed-preview-url?expiresInSeconds=N
```

This is the call to prefer when you want to hand someone a working link and keep the box private. The signature is what authorizes the request, so the recipient needs no API key and you never flip the public flag — the box stays closed to everyone who does not hold the link, and the link stops working on its own.

`expiresInSeconds` is an optional query parameter, and **the default is 60 seconds**. Sixty seconds is the right size for a link your own code generates and redirects to immediately; pass a larger value when a person has to open it, read it, and click around.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
BOXLITE_REST_URL="${BOXLITE_REST_URL:-https://api.boxlite.ai}"

# 900 seconds gives a reviewer a quarter of an hour with the link
curl -fsS \
  "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/box/review-app-142/ports/8080/signed-preview-url?expiresInSeconds=900" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${BOXLITE_API_KEY}" | jq -r '.url, .token'
```

A `200` returns:

| Field | Type | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `boxId` | string | The box the URL points at |
| `port` | number | The port inside the box that the URL addresses |
| `token` | string | Identifies this signed URL. Keep it — revoking the URL needs it |
| `url` | string | The signed address, shaped `https://{port}-{token}.{proxyDomain}` |

Generate a fresh signed URL per recipient and per sharing session rather than reusing one. Each is independently revocable, so one leaked link is one link you can kill.

### Revoke a signed URL before it expires

```http theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
POST /api/box/{boxIdOrName}/ports/{port}/signed-preview-url/{token}/expire
```

The `token` in the path is the `token` field from the signed-URL response — that is the reason to keep it rather than discarding everything but the `url`. A `200` returns no body.

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
BOXLITE_REST_URL="${BOXLITE_REST_URL:-https://api.boxlite.ai}"
SIGNED_TOKEN="<TOKEN_FROM_THE_SIGNED_URL_RESPONSE>"

curl -fsS -X POST \
  "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/box/review-app-142/ports/8080/signed-preview-url/${SIGNED_TOKEN}/expire" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${BOXLITE_API_KEY}"
```

Revoke as soon as the review is over, the demo ends, or the link lands somewhere you did not intend. Waiting for an expiry you set generously is a choice to stay exposed.

### Choose between the three

| Approach | Who can reach the box | Suits |
| - | - | - |
| Private box, SDK tunnel | Only code holding your API key | Your own program as the client, any TCP protocol, agent traffic that should never be addressable from outside |
| Private box, signed preview URL | Anyone holding the link, until it expires or you revoke it | A preview for a reviewer, a teammate, or an end user; a link your app generates per session |
| Public box | Anyone holding any URL to the box, until you set the flag back | A demo you are content to have indexed, crawled, and forwarded |

The order matters: start private, escalate to a signed URL when a human needs to see something, and reserve the public flag for a box whose contents you would publish deliberately.

## Outbound: what the box can reach

Outbound is a per-box setting you make at creation, not a toggle you flip afterwards. Pass a `NetworkSpec` as the `network` field of `BoxOptions`, and the SDK sends that specification — the mode and the allowlist — to Cloud as part of the create call.

There are exactly two modes, `enabled` and `disabled`, plus the `allow_net` allowlist that narrows egress to named hosts. The `NetworkSpec` parameter table, the useful mode and allowlist combinations, and the verification recipe live on [Network access](/manage-sandbox/network-access), which owns them.

One property of the allowlist decides whether you can debug it. **A host outside the allowlist is a DNS sinkhole, not a connection error: it resolves to `0.0.0.0`.** Your code therefore reports a failed connection to `0.0.0.0` rather than a refusal or a policy message, and a `nslookup` of a blocked host can still exit `0` because the lookup itself succeeded. Read the resolved address, never the exit code, when you want to know what a box's DNS returned for a host.

```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
# cloud_egress_allowlist.py — create a Cloud box with an outbound allowlist
# Run: python cloud_egress_allowlist.py
import asyncio
import os
import time

from boxlite import (
    ApiKeyCredential,
    Boxlite,
    BoxliteRestOptions,
    BoxOptions,
    NetworkSpec,
    OutboundNetworkSpec,
)

IMAGE = "ghcr.io/boxlite-ai/boxlite-agent-base:v0.1.0"

# The hosts this box is meant to talk to. Everything else is left off the list.
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["pypi.org", "files.pythonhosted.org"]


async def resolve(box, host: str) -> str:
    """Run nslookup inside the box and return its stdout."""
    execution = await box.exec("nslookup", args=[host])
    output = ""
    async for line in execution.stdout():
        output += line
    await execution.wait()  # exit code says nothing about a sinkhole
    return output


async def main() -> None:
    # export BOXLITE_API_KEY=<YOUR_API_KEY> before running
    rt = Boxlite.rest(BoxliteRestOptions(
        url=os.environ.get("BOXLITE_REST_URL", "https://api.boxlite.ai"),
        credential=ApiKeyCredential(os.environ["BOXLITE_API_KEY"]),
    ))

    box_id = None
    try:
        box = await rt.create(
            BoxOptions(
                image=IMAGE,
                network=NetworkSpec(outbound=OutboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled", allow_net=ALLOWED_HOSTS)),
            ),
            name=f"egress-allowlist-{int(time.time())}",
        )
        box_id = box.id
        await box.start()

        # Read the resolved address for a listed host and an unlisted one.
        for host in ("pypi.org", "example.com"):
            print(f"--- nslookup {host} ---")
            print(await resolve(box, host))
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"allowlist demo failed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
    finally:
        # Teardown on the runtime, in finally, so a failure above leaves nothing running.
        if box_id:
            try:
                await rt.remove(box_id, force=True)
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"remove failed: {exc}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

`mode="disabled"` is the other end of the range. The mode means a box with no network interface at all: DNS and every outbound connection fail, while commands and file operations work as normal. That is the mode to ask for when a box's only job is to run code you do not trust with a network. [Network access](/manage-sandbox/network-access) documents both modes in full.

One more thing to know about a box you did not configure yourself. A box created without a `network` field inherits your organization's default, and that default can be limited egress rather than open egress — so a box that resolves fewer hosts than you expect may be following the organization default rather than misbehaving. That default is set at the platform level; it is not a field of `BoxOptions` and not part of the boxes API.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| - | - | - |
| Fetching a preview URL returns unauthorized | The box is private, and the request carried no credential that the preview proxy accepts | Choose deliberately: issue a signed preview URL for the port, or set the box public with `POST /api/box/{boxIdOrName}/public/true` and accept that anyone with a URL can reach it |
| A signed URL that worked a minute ago now fails | Its lifetime elapsed — the default is 60 seconds when you omit `expiresInSeconds` — or the token was revoked through the expire route | Request a new signed URL, passing an `expiresInSeconds` that matches how long a person actually needs |
| A signed URL fails immediately after you issue it | The token was already revoked, or the URL was truncated in transit through a chat client or ticket field | Issue a fresh signed URL and paste the whole `url` value, including its token |
| The preview URL loads but nothing answers, or the connection is refused | The service inside the box is bound to `127.0.0.1`, so traffic arriving on the box's network interface cannot reach it | Bind `0.0.0.0` — `python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0`, Flask `app.run(host="0.0.0.0")`, uvicorn `--host 0.0.0.0`. Background: [Network](/cloud/network) |
| The first request to a stopped box hangs for about half a minute, then returns `503 {"message":"box is starting; retry shortly"}` with `Retry-After: 3` | **That request woke the box.** A preview request no longer fails against a stopped box — it starts it, waits, and tells you when to come back if the box is not ready in time | Honour `Retry-After` and retry. Raise or disable the idle timeout for a box that must answer immediately — see [Stop when idle](/cloud/box-lifecycle#stop-when-idle) |
| `502 {"message":"box unreachable","code":"BAD_GATEWAY"}` right after a box wakes | The box is running again, but the service inside it is not. A process you started with `exec` does not come back by itself — only the box's main command does | Start your service as the box's **main command** rather than with `exec`, so waking the box is enough to serve it. See [The main command](/manage-sandbox/lifecycle#the-main-command) |
| `404 {"message":"not found: tunnel not found"}` from a preview URL | No tunnel is open on that port. Being handed a URL does not open one | Open a tunnel for the port — see [Get a preview URL for a port](#get-a-preview-url-for-a-port) |
| The preview URL answers for one port and 404s for another | A preview URL addresses a single port. The second port needs its own | Fetch `GET /api/box/{boxIdOrName}/ports/{port}/preview-url` again with the other port number |
| An outbound request in the box connects to `0.0.0.0` and fails there | The host is not on the box's `allow_net` list, and a blocked host is sinkholed rather than refused | Add the host to `allow_net` when the box legitimately needs it. Verify by reading the resolved address, not the exit code — see [Network access](/manage-sandbox/network-access) |
| `nslookup` of a blocked host exits `0`, so a script treats it as reachable | The lookup succeeded; it just answered `0.0.0.0` | Test the resolved address in your script, for example by checking whether the output contains `0.0.0.0` |
| Opening a tunnel fails with `Box ${boxId} is not public; set public: true before opening a tunnel`, on code that used to work | Inbound has defaulted to `disabled` since 0.10.5, and the flat `NetworkSpec(mode=...)` configures outbound only | Create the box with `inbound=InboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled")`, or flip the existing box with the public flag — see [A new box is private](#a-new-box-is-private) |
| `InvalidArgumentError: ... inbound.allow_net is not supported yet` | An inbound allowlist was passed. Inbound is governed by `mode` alone | Drop `allow_net` from the `InboundNetworkSpec`. To admit one audience rather than everyone, keep the box private and issue a signed URL |
| The public flag call returns forbidden | The key's holder lacks write access to boxes in your organization | Use a credential with write access to boxes, or ask whoever administers the organization to make the change |
| A box resolves fewer hosts than you expect, and you passed no `network` field | The box inherited your organization's default for limited outbound egress | Pass an explicit `NetworkSpec` with the hosts the box needs, so the box's egress is stated in your code rather than inherited |

## Next steps

>

# Wallet or a plan?
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/plans

Two ways to fund usage on BoxLite Cloud, the usage level at which a subscription starts costing less than paying from your wallet, and the concurrency limit that is not a money question at all.

Usage on BoxLite Cloud can be funded two ways: from a prepaid **wallet** alone, or from a **plan** whose included quota covers usage first and whose wallet picks up the rest. Which one costs less is arithmetic, and it turns on a single number — your monthly usage.

## How funding works

**Quota covers first, the wallet funds the rest.** A box draws on this cycle's included quota until the quota is gone, and on your prepaid wallet balance from then on.

An account does not have to carry a plan. With no plan there is no included quota, and every dollar of usage comes straight out of the wallet — pay-as-you-go, in the ordinary sense.

## The plans

Each plan buys more usage than it costs, which is where the saving comes from:

| Plan | Price | Included quota | Concurrency limit | Saving past quota |
| - | - | - | - | - |
| Starter | \$19/mo | \$30 | 20 boxes | \$11/mo |
| Pro | \$149/mo | \$250 | 100 boxes | \$101/mo |
| Max | \$499/mo | \$900 | 1000 boxes | \$401/mo |

The last column is the quota minus the price. Once your usage passes a plan's quota, that is exactly what the plan saves you against paying full price from the wallet, every month.

**Enterprise** is negotiated rather than self-serve: custom limits and compliance review, arranged through [sales@boxlite.ai](mailto:sales@boxlite.ai). A negotiated plan carries no public price, and an unlimited quota or concurrency shows as unlimited rather than as a number.

## Which one costs less

Look up what the console reports as spent this month, and three thresholds decide it:

| When your monthly usage passes | Move to | Because |
| - | - | - |
| **\$20** | Starter | Starter's $19 buys $30 of usage |
| **\$161** | Pro | Pro's flat $149 beats Starter's $150 at this point |
| **\$601** | Max | Max's flat $499 beats Pro's $500 at this point |

The first threshold is a plan's own price: past $20 of usage, Starter's flat $19 beats paying full price from the wallet. The other two are crossovers against the **previous plan's total cost** at that usage level, not against their own price — Starter's $19 plus overage reaches Pro's flat $149 at $160, and Pro's reaches Max's at $600. Below a plan's own price you are buying quota you will not use.

These thresholds assume a typical month. If your usage swings — a heavy month followed by a quiet one — the plan price is charged either way, so size against your *steady* level rather than your peak.

## Concurrency is a separate decision

Concurrency caps how many boxes run **at the same time** — not how many you create over a month, and not how much work each one does. It is independent of quota: you can hit the limit with quota to spare, and exhaust quota while running a single box.

If you are building an agent fleet, size against your fan-out. An orchestrator that runs 40 parallel agents, one box each, needs a plan whose limit clears 40 — Starter's 20 will stall it halfway through the batch.

So concurrency alone can push you onto a larger plan well before the money says to move. A fleet of 40 short-lived Small boxes might spend \$60 a month — Starter territory on cost — while needing Pro's 100-box limit to run at all.

## Changing plans

The direction of the change decides when it lands and what you are charged:

| Change | When it applies | What you are charged now |
| - | - | - |
| **Upgrade** | Immediately, and the new quota is available right away | The prorated difference, today |
| **Downgrade** | At the next cycle roll | Nothing |
| **Cancel** | At the end of the cycle you have paid for | Nothing |
| **Subscribe** (from no plan) | As soon as payment is confirmed | The plan price, through Stripe checkout |

Two details worth knowing before you act:

* **A downgrade does not cost you this cycle's quota.** The quota you already paid for stays available until the cycle rolls, along with the current plan's concurrency limit.
* **A queued change can be called off.** While a downgrade or cancellation is scheduled, the console offers to keep your current plan instead, which discards the queued change.

## Troubleshooting

| Situation | Why it happens | What to do |
| - | - | - |
| New boxes are refused while your existing boxes keep running fine | You are at your plan's concurrency limit — the cap is on boxes running simultaneously, not on boxes created | Stop or delete a box to free a slot, or move to a plan with a higher limit |
| Cost is showing as wallet-funded rather than quota-covered | This cycle's included quota is consumed, so usage now draws on the prepaid balance | Nothing is broken. Keep the wallet funded, or move to a plan whose quota matches your steady-state usage |
| Your plan shows as having no subscription | The account carries no plan, so there is no included quota and no plan concurrency limit | Pick a plan, or keep running on wallet balance alone if your usage is below \$20/mo |
| A plan change you scheduled has not happened | Downgrades and cancellations apply at the cycle roll, not immediately | Check the cycle end date. To act sooner, upgrade instead — upgrades apply immediately |
| Switching away from your current plan is refused | Your plan is negotiated rather than self-serve, so it has no catalog price to switch against | Talk to [sales@boxlite.ai](mailto:sales@boxlite.ai) before changing |

## Next steps

> [card] [What a box costs](/cloud/box-costs)
>
> The hourly rates behind every dollar figure on this page.

> [card] [Managing billing](/cloud/billing)
>
> Top up the wallet, set automatic reload, and read the usage chart.


# Forward a box port to a local port
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/port-forwarding

Publish a port inside a Cloud box on an address on your own machine, so any TCP client can reach it without knowing about BoxLite.

Some clients cannot be taught to speak through an SDK — `curl`, a browser, a database driver, an existing library that only knows how to dial a socket. `forward()` publishes the tunnel on a local address so all of them just work.

## Prerequisites

* An API key from the console, exported as `BOXLITE_API_KEY`. See [API keys](/cloud/api-keys).
* `pip install boxlite`, and the REST URL exported as `BOXLITE_REST_URL`. See [Quickstart](/cloud/quickstart).
* A box you can start, and a service inside it that listens on a TCP port.
* **The box must be created with inbound enabled.** A tunnel against a private
  box is refused, and inbound has defaulted to `disabled` since 0.10.5 — see
  [Network policy](/cloud/network-policy#a-new-box-is-private).

Every example reads both values from the environment, so nothing hard-codes a credential.

## Publish a box port on your machine

> [tab] CLI
>
> One command, and it stays in the foreground forwarding until you stop it:
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> boxlite network tunnel mybox 18080 --listen 127.0.0.1:18080
> # tcp://127.0.0.1:18080
> ```
>
> Reach for this when you just need the port open while you work — no script to write,
> nothing to clean up. Flags are on the [CLI reference](/reference/cli#boxlite-network).

> [tab] SDK
>
> `forward()` publishes the tunnel on an address on your machine, so any TCP client can
> reach the service without knowing about BoxLite. Use this when the forward is part of
> something your program does, and it has to pick the port, hand it to something else,
> or shut down cleanly.

The script below is the SDK path end to end — start a service in a box, forward it, and
fetch it from the local address:

```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
# cloud_tunnel_forward.py — publish a box port on a local port
# Run: python cloud_tunnel_forward.py
import asyncio
import os
import time
import urllib.request

from boxlite import (
    ApiKeyCredential,
    Boxlite,
    BoxliteRestOptions,
    BoxOptions,
    InboundNetworkSpec,
    NetworkSpec,
    SocketAddress,
)

GUEST_PORT = 18080
IMAGE = "ghcr.io/boxlite-ai/boxlite-agent-base:v0.1.0"


async def main() -> None:
    # export BOXLITE_API_KEY=<YOUR_API_KEY> before running
    rt = Boxlite.rest(BoxliteRestOptions(
        url=os.environ.get("BOXLITE_REST_URL", "https://api.boxlite.ai"),
        credential=ApiKeyCredential(os.environ["BOXLITE_API_KEY"]),
    ))

    box_id = None
    forwarder = None
    try:
        box = await rt.create(
            BoxOptions(
                image=IMAGE,
                # Required for a tunnel: inbound is disabled by default,
                # and a tunnel against a private box is refused.
                network=NetworkSpec(inbound=InboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled")),
            ),
            name=f"tunnel-forward-{int(time.time())}",
        )
        box_id = box.id
        await box.start()

        launch = await box.exec("sh", args=[
            "-c",
            f"nohup python3 -m http.server {GUEST_PORT} --bind 0.0.0.0 "
            "> /tmp/server.log 2>&1 & echo launched",
        ])
        await launch.wait()
        await asyncio.sleep(2)  # give the server time to bind

        # host must be a numeric IP; port=0 asks the OS for a free port.
        listener = SocketAddress.tcp(host="127.0.0.1", port=0)

        tunnel = await box.network.tunnel(GUEST_PORT)
        forwarder = await tunnel.forward(listener)  # consumes the tunnel

        local = forwarder.local_addr()  # synchronous
        print(f"forwarding 127.0.0.1:{local.port} -> box port {GUEST_PORT}")

        # Any TCP client can now dial the local address. urllib is blocking,
        # so run it off the event loop.
        def fetch() -> int:
            url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{local.port}/"
            with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as resp:
                return resp.status

        print(f"local request status: {await asyncio.to_thread(fetch)}")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"forward demo failed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
    finally:
        if forwarder is not None:
            try:
                await forwarder.close()
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"forwarder close failed: {exc}")
        if box_id:
            try:
                await rt.remove(box_id, force=True)
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"remove failed: {exc}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

## Choose the listening address

Three constraints, each of which raises rather than failing quietly:

* The host must be a **numeric IP**. `SocketAddress.tcp(host="localhost")` raises `ValueError: tunnel listener host must be a numeric IP` — pass `"127.0.0.1"`.
* `port=0` is the default and asks the operating system for a free port. Read the port you actually got from `forwarder.local_addr().port`.
* A Unix socket path must be **absolute**. `SocketAddress.unix("relative.sock")` raises `ValueError: tunnel Unix socket path must be absolute`.

## Keep it running, and shut it down

`await forwarder.wait()` blocks until the forwarder finishes — that is what a
long-running process awaits instead of exiting. `await forwarder.close()` shuts it down.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **`forward()` spends the tunnel it was built from.** Build each forwarder from its own
> fresh `await box.network.tunnel(port)`; reusing one will not work.

## Next steps

> [card] [Network](/cloud/network)
>
> How tunnels work, the full parameter reference, and the outbound boundary.

> [card] [Network policy](/cloud/network-policy)
>
> Control what the box itself is allowed to reach.


# Pricing
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/pricing

What BoxLite Cloud charges for: three metered resources billed by the hour, funded by a prepaid wallet or a plan's included quota.

BoxLite Cloud meters three things, by the hour:

| Resource | Unit | Rate |
| - | - | - |
| vCPU | per vCPU-hour | **\$0.0504** |
| Memory | per GiB-hour | **\$0.0144** |
| Disk | per GiB-hour | **\$0.00018** |

Nothing else is metered — no charge for network traffic, API requests, mounted volumes, preview URLs, or boot time. There is no minimum billable duration and no rounding up to the hour.

Usage is funded by a prepaid **wallet**, or by a **plan** whose included quota is consumed first.

> [card] [Wallet or a plan?](/cloud/plans)
>
> Plan tiers, and the usage level at which a subscription starts costing less.

>
> Top up, set automatic reload, and read what you were actually charged.

# Use a private image
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/private-images

Register one registry login so BoxLite can pull your private images, and know which images that login covers.

Most images need nothing from you. A private one needs a login BoxLite can pull with — registered once per registry, after which referencing it is identical to [any other image](/cloud/use-your-image):

```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
box = await rt.create(
    BoxOptions(image="ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.0"),
    name="demo",
)
```

No credentials at the call site, ever. Which login gets used is worked out from the reference.

## Which images a login covers

An image reference has three parts, and a login is registered against the first one:

```text theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
ghcr.io / acme/api : 1.4.0
   │         │        └── tag
   │         └── repository
   └── registry host    ← the login is for this
```

You can narrow it to part of the registry with a **repository prefix**:

| Registered as | Covers |
| - | - |
| `ghcr.io`, no prefix | Every private image on `ghcr.io` |
| `ghcr.io` + `acme/` | `ghcr.io/acme/api`, `ghcr.io/acme/worker`, … not `ghcr.io/other/x` |
| `ghcr.io` + `acme/team-a/` | Only what is under `acme/team-a/` |

When several logins could match, **the most specific one wins**. So a broad `acme/` login can cover an organization while `acme/team-a/` overrides it for one team.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A prefix is whole path segments and must end in `/`. `acme/` is accepted; `acme` is refused. Omit it to cover the whole registry.

A login can be registered for `ghcr.io`, `docker.io`, `quay.io`, and Google Container Registry — `gcr.io` and its `us.`, `eu.`, and `asia.` hosts. Any other host is refused when you create the login.

### What goes in username and password

BoxLite signs in the same way everywhere — a username and a password or token. What those two values *are* is each registry's own convention, and getting them wrong is the usual reason a pull fails with `UNAUTHORIZED`.

| Registry | `username` | `password` |
| - | - | - |
| `ghcr.io` | Your GitHub username | A [classic personal access token](https://docs.github.com/en/packages/working-with-a-github-packages-registry/working-with-the-container-registry) with the `read:packages` scope |
| `docker.io` | Your Docker Hub username | A [Docker Hub access token](https://docs.docker.com/security/for-developers/access-tokens/) with read-only permission |
| `quay.io` | A [robot account](https://docs.quay.io/glossary/robot-accounts.html) name, like `acme+puller` | That robot account's token |
| `gcr.io` and its regional hosts | `_json_key` | The whole [service account JSON key](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs/docker/authentication), as one string |

> [!NOTE]
>
> For Google, `oauth2accesstoken` with a short-lived access token also works, but the token expires — a service account key is what you want for a login BoxLite keeps.

Your own account's password is never the right answer. Every registry above issues a token meant for exactly this, and each can be scoped to read-only.

## Register the login

> [tab] Console
>
> 1. Open **Images**, then the **Private registries** tab.
> 2. Click **Connect a registry**.
> 3. Fill in the host, your username, and a password or access token. Add a repository prefix if you want to narrow it.
>
> The table then lists the host, what it covers, the username, and when it was added.
>
> This is the easier path for a one-time setup, and the only one that does not need a Full-access API key.

> [tab] SDK
>
> ```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> await rt.images.registries.create(
>     registry_host="ghcr.io",
>     username="<YOUR_REGISTRY_USERNAME>",
>     password="<YOUR_REGISTRY_TOKEN>",
>     repository_prefix="acme/",      # optional
> )
> ```
>
> Use this when the login has to be created without a person — provisioning a new environment, say. It needs a key with **Full** access.

Use a read-only pull token where your registry issues one. BoxLite only ever pulls.

## Then start boxes as usual

With the login in place, a private reference behaves exactly like a public one. It is recorded in [the catalog](/cloud/image-catalog) once the box boots, counts against the same limit, and can carry [aliases](/cloud/image-aliases).

## Review or remove a login

> [tab] Console
>
> The **Private registries** tab lists every login with its host, coverage, and username, and removes one from the row's action menu.

> [tab] SDK
>
> ```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> registries = await rt.images.registries.list()
> await rt.images.registries.remove(login_id)
> ```

Removing a login leaves images already in the catalog alone. New boxes that needed it fail to pull.

## Things that will bite you

* **The password is write-only.** Nothing ever reads it back — not the console, not the SDK. Rotating a credential means removing the login and creating it again; there is no update.
* **A prefix without a trailing `/` is refused.** `acme/`, not `acme`.
* **Forbidden errors on registry calls are a key problem.** These calls need **Full** access; a **Boxes** key cannot make them.

## Next

> [card] [Pin a build](/cloud/image-aliases)
>
> Name the exact build production should boot.

> [card] [The catalog](/cloud/image-catalog)
>
> Private images count against the same limit as public ones.


# Run untrusted code on BoxLite Cloud
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/quickstart

Create an API key, point the SDK at BoxLite Cloud, and run a command inside a hardware-isolated box — no local virtualization, no daemon, three steps.

BoxLite Cloud runs your boxes on BoxLite's own resource pool, so the machine that calls the API needs nothing but a URL and an API key. Untrusted code still lands inside a microVM with hardware-level isolation — you no longer operate the hypervisor underneath it.

## Prerequisites

| Prerequisite | Notes |
| - | - |
| A BoxLite Cloud account | Sign in to the console at `https://app.boxlite.ai`. |
| An API key | Created in the console — step 1 below. |
| Python 3, Node, or `curl` + `jq` | Whichever tab you follow in step 3. |

**1. Create an API key**

In the console, open **API Keys** and click **Create Key**. Give it a name such as `sdk-quickstart` and leave **Expires** at its default of `No expiration` while you are exploring.

The key looks like `blk_live_...` and is shown in full exactly once, at creation. Copy it then — the list view only ever shows a masked form afterwards. A key grants access to the Boxes API: it can create and manage boxes, and shared Linux base images are available to it automatically.

For key rotation, per-environment keys, and the CLI credential store, see [API keys and authentication](/cloud/api-keys).

**2. Install the SDK or CLI**

> [tab] Python
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> pip install boxlite
> ```

> [tab] Node
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> npm install @boxlite-ai/boxlite tsx
> ```
>
> The Node client construction for Cloud is shown in [Give the key to your code](/cloud/api-keys#give-the-key-to-your-code).

> [tab] CLI
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> curl -fsSL https://sh.boxlite.ai | sh
> ```

> [tab] REST (curl)
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> # The REST tab needs no SDK — only curl and jq
> curl --version
> jq --version
> ```

Then export your credentials. Read the key interactively so it never lands in your shell history:

```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
read -rs BOXLITE_API_KEY   # prompts without echoing; paste your blk_live_... key
export BOXLITE_API_KEY
export BOXLITE_REST_URL="https://api.boxlite.ai"
```

**3. Create a box and run code in it**

> [tab] Python
>
> ```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> # cloud_quickstart.py — create a box on BoxLite Cloud, run a command, tear it down
> # Run: python cloud_quickstart.py
> import asyncio
> import os
> import time
>
> from boxlite import (
>     ApiKeyCredential,
>     Boxlite,
>     BoxOptions,
>     BoxliteRestOptions,
> )
>
> api_key = os.environ.get("BOXLITE_API_KEY")
> if not api_key:
>     raise SystemExit("Set BOXLITE_API_KEY to your blk_live_... key before running this.")
>
>
> async def main() -> None:
>     # Boxlite.rest(...) is a synchronous constructor; every runtime method below is awaited
>     rt = Boxlite.rest(
>         BoxliteRestOptions(
>             url=os.environ.get("BOXLITE_REST_URL", "https://api.boxlite.ai"),
>             credential=ApiKeyCredential(api_key),
>         )
>     )
>
>     box = None
>     try:
>         # name is an argument of rt.create(), not a field of BoxOptions
>         box = await rt.create(
>             BoxOptions(image="ghcr.io/boxlite-ai/boxlite-agent-base:v0.1.0"),
>             name=f"sdk-quickstart-python-{int(time.time())}",
>         )
>         await box.start()
>         print(f"Created box: {box.id}")
>
>         # Over REST, exec takes the command plus an args list
>         execution = await box.exec("echo", args=["Hello from BoxLite SDK"])
>
>         output = ""
>         async for line in execution.stdout():
>             output += line
>
>         result = await execution.wait()
>         print(f"Exit code: {result.exit_code}")
>         print(output)
>     except Exception as exc:
>         # Authentication failures, network errors and creation failures all surface here
>         print(f"Cloud run failed: {exc!r}")
>     finally:
>         # Teardown lives on the runtime. Putting it in finally means a failure above
>         # cannot leave a box running and billing.
>         if box is not None:
>             await rt.remove(box.id, force=True)
>             print(f"Removed {box.id}")
>
>
> if __name__ == "__main__":
>     asyncio.run(main())
> ```

> [tab] Node
>
> ```typescript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> // cloud_quickstart.ts — create a box on BoxLite Cloud, run a command, tear it down
> // Run: npx tsx cloud_quickstart.ts
> import {
>   ApiKeyCredential,
>   BoxliteRestOptions,
>   JsBoxlite,
> } from "@boxlite-ai/boxlite";
>
> async function main(): Promise<void> {
>   const apiKey = process.env.BOXLITE_API_KEY;
>   if (!apiKey) {
>     throw new Error("Set BOXLITE_API_KEY to your blk_live_... key before running this.");
>   }
>
>   // JsBoxlite.rest(...) is a synchronous constructor; every runtime method below is awaited
>   const rt = JsBoxlite.rest(
>     new BoxliteRestOptions({
>       url: process.env.BOXLITE_REST_URL ?? "https://api.boxlite.ai",
>       credential: new ApiKeyCredential(apiKey),
>     }),
>   );
>
>   let boxId: string | null = null;
>   try {
>     // The box name is the second argument of create(), not a field of the options object
>     const box = await rt.create(
>       { image: "ghcr.io/boxlite-ai/boxlite-agent-base:v0.1.0" },
>       `sdk-quickstart-node-${Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)}`,
>     );
>     boxId = box.id;
>     await box.start();
>     console.log(`Created box: ${box.id}`);
>
>     // Over REST, exec takes the command plus an args array
>     const execution = await box.exec("echo", ["Hello from BoxLite SDK"]);
>
>     // A stream is consumed once; iterate until next() returns null
>     const stdout = await execution.stdout();
>     let output = "";
>     while (true) {
>       const line = await stdout.next();
>       if (line === null) break;
>       output += line;
>     }
>
>     const result = await execution.wait();
>     console.log(`Exit code: ${result.exitCode}`);
>     console.log(output);
>   } catch (err) {
>     // Authentication failures, network errors and creation failures all surface here
>     console.error("Cloud run failed:", err);
>   } finally {
>     // Teardown lives on the runtime, so a failure above cannot leave a box running
>     if (boxId !== null) {
>       await rt.remove(boxId, true);
>       console.log(`Removed ${boxId}`);
>     }
>     rt.close();
>   }
> }
>
> main();
> ```
>
> Two call shapes differ from Python: `exec` takes its argument list positionally (`box.exec("echo", ["hi"])`), and a stdout stream is pulled with `next()` until it returns `null` rather than iterated with `for await`. Field names are camelCase throughout — `result.exitCode`, and `diskSizeGb` / `memoryMib` on the options object.

> [tab] CLI
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> # One disposable box, one command, automatic teardown.
> # --rm removes the box once the command exits.
> boxlite run --rm --name "sdk-quickstart-cli-$(date +%s)" \
>   ghcr.io/boxlite-ai/boxlite-agent-base:v0.1.0 \
>   echo "Hello from BoxLite CLI"
> ```
>
> `boxlite` talks to Cloud whenever REST configuration is present in the environment, which the `BOXLITE_REST_URL` and `BOXLITE_API_KEY` exports from step 2 provide. The CLI exit code is the exit code of the command you ran. To store credentials once instead of exporting them per shell, see [API keys and authentication](/cloud/api-keys#persist-credentials-for-the-cli).

> [tab] REST (curl)
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> #!/usr/bin/env bash
> # cloud_quickstart.sh — create a box on BoxLite Cloud, run a command, tear it down
> set -euo pipefail
>
> BOXLITE_REST_URL="${BOXLITE_REST_URL:-https://api.boxlite.ai}"
> : "${BOXLITE_API_KEY:?Set BOXLITE_API_KEY to your blk_live_... key before running this}"
>
> auth=(-H "Authorization: Bearer ${BOXLITE_API_KEY}")
> json=(-H "Content-Type: application/json")
> name="sdk-quickstart-rest-$(date +%s)"
>
> # Create — the response carries the new box in the box_id field
> box_id="$(curl -fsS -X POST "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/v1/boxes" \
>   "${auth[@]}" "${json[@]}" \
>   -d "{\"name\":\"${name}\",\"image\":\"ghcr.io/boxlite-ai/boxlite-agent-base:v0.1.0\"}" \
>   | jq -r '.box_id')"
> echo "Created box: ${box_id}"
>
> # Remove the box on any exit, so a failure below cannot leave it running
> trap 'curl -fsS -X DELETE "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/v1/boxes/${box_id}?force=true" "${auth[@]}" >/dev/null' EXIT
>
> curl -fsS -X POST "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/v1/boxes/${box_id}/start" "${auth[@]}"
>
> # Exec — the response carries the execution in the execution_id field
> exec_id="$(curl -fsS -X POST "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/v1/boxes/${box_id}/exec" \
>   "${auth[@]}" "${json[@]}" \
>   -d '{"command":"echo","args":["Hello from BoxLite REST"]}' \
>   | jq -r '.execution_id')"
>
> # Read the execution record back
> curl -fsS "${BOXLITE_REST_URL}/v1/boxes/${box_id}/executions/${exec_id}" "${auth[@]}"
> ```
>
> Run it with `bash cloud_quickstart.sh`. Every path is relative to `BOXLITE_REST_URL`, so the create call above resolves to `https://api.boxlite.ai/v1/boxes`.

## What just happened

The five calls in that script are the whole Cloud lifecycle. Every language binding and the REST API expose the same five, in the same order:

1. **Authenticate.** `Boxlite.rest(...)` wraps your key in an `ApiKeyCredential` and points every later call at `https://api.boxlite.ai`. Nothing is sent at construction time — the object is just a configured client.
2. **Create.** `rt.create(BoxOptions(image=...), name=...)` allocates a box from a shared Linux base image and returns a handle. On Cloud the box is already running by the time this returns — `POST /v1/boxes` answers with `status: running`, and reading the box back before any other call reports the same.
3. **Start.** `box.start()` is what boots the microVM on a self-hosted runtime. On Cloud the box is up already, so the call confirms that state rather than changing it: it is safe to repeat, and returns the box still `running`. Keeping it in the script is what lets the same five calls run against either runtime.
4. **Exec.** `box.exec("echo", args=[...])` launches one process inside the VM and hands you an execution handle. `execution.wait()` blocks until that process exits and returns its exit code.
5. **Remove.** `rt.remove(box.id, force=True)` destroys the box and its disk. Removal is a **runtime** method, not a box method — the box handle you hold is a pointer, and the runtime owns the fleet.

Step 5 is the one to internalize. A box you forget to remove keeps running, and a running box is what BoxLite Cloud charges for — see [What a box costs](/cloud/box-costs). Putting teardown in a `finally` block, as the script above does, is the difference between an exception costing you a stack trace and an exception costing you a box.

## Expected output

```text theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
Created box: <box-id>
Exit code: 0
Hello from BoxLite SDK
Removed <box-id>
```

The `Exit code` line comes from `execution.wait()` and is the authoritative success signal. The `Hello from BoxLite SDK` line is what the box wrote to stdout, collected by iterating `execution.stdout()`.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| - | - | - |
| `401 Unauthorized` on the first call | The key is missing, mistyped, or was deleted in the console. | Confirm the value starts with `blk_live_` and matches a live key in **API Keys**. See [API keys and authentication](/cloud/api-keys#troubleshooting). |
| `SystemExit: Set BOXLITE_API_KEY ...`, or the CLI uses your local runtime instead of Cloud | The key never reached the process — a new shell, a different terminal tab, or a service manager that does not inherit your exports. | Re-run the `read -rs` and `export` pair from step 2 in that shell. For anything long-lived, store the credential with `boxlite auth login` instead of exporting it. |
| A box from an earlier run is still listed as running | The script exited before teardown — an exception outside `try`, a `Ctrl-C`, or a crash. | Remove it explicitly with `await rt.remove("<BOX_ID_OR_NAME>", force=True)` (CLI: `boxlite rm`), then move teardown into a `finally` block as shown above. |
| A long job stops part-way through with no error from your code | The box was stopped for being idle, and work running *inside* the box does not count as activity. | Adjust **STOP WHEN IDLE** when you create the box in the console — see [Stop when idle](/cloud/box-lifecycle#stop-when-idle). |
| `execution.stdout()` finishes without yielding lines | Streamed output is a separate channel from the exit code. Only `execution.wait()` is guaranteed to report the process result. | Treat `result.exit_code` as the success signal and collect output as a bonus. When you need output you can depend on, redirect it to a file in the box and read the file back. |
| An HTML page comes back instead of JSON, and the status is `200` | The base URL points at the console host `https://app.boxlite.ai` instead of the API host. The console answers unrecognised paths with the dashboard page, so a wrong base URL returns markup rather than an error. | Set `BOXLITE_REST_URL` to exactly `https://api.boxlite.ai`. |

# Read and write raw bytes over a tunnel
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/raw-streams

Drive a tunnel as a bidirectional byte stream when you are speaking a protocol of your own rather than HTTP.

A tunnel moves bytes and interprets nothing along the way. When your service speaks a protocol of its own, take the connection directly and read and write it yourself.

## Prerequisites

* An API key from the console, exported as `BOXLITE_API_KEY`. See [API keys](/cloud/api-keys).
* `pip install boxlite`, and the REST URL exported as `BOXLITE_REST_URL`. See [Quickstart](/cloud/quickstart).
* A box you can start, and a service inside it that listens on a TCP port.
* **The box must be created with inbound enabled.** A tunnel against a private
  box is refused, and inbound has defaulted to `disabled` since 0.10.5 — see
  [Network policy](/cloud/network-policy#a-new-box-is-private).

Every example reads both values from the environment, so nothing hard-codes a credential.

## Take the connection yourself

`connect()` hands you the byte stream directly. This is the level you work at for a
protocol that is not HTTP — a line protocol, a binary framing, a database wire
protocol — or when you want full control over what goes on the wire.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **`connect()` spends the tunnel.** So does `forward()`. Build a fresh
> `await box.network.tunnel(port)` for each connection you need; only `uri()` leaves a
> tunnel reusable.

```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
# cloud_tunnel_bytes.py — talk to a non-HTTP TCP service inside a box
# Run: python cloud_tunnel_bytes.py
import asyncio
import os
import shlex
import time

from boxlite import (
    ApiKeyCredential,
    Boxlite,
    BoxliteRestOptions,
    BoxOptions,
    InboundNetworkSpec,
    NetworkSpec,
)

GUEST_PORT = 18090
IMAGE = "ghcr.io/boxlite-ai/boxlite-agent-base:v0.1.0"

# A line protocol: read one newline-terminated line, reply with it upper-cased.
SERVER_CODE = f"""
import socketserver

class Handler(socketserver.StreamRequestHandler):
    def handle(self):
        line = self.rfile.readline()
        self.wfile.write(line.upper())

class Server(socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer):
    allow_reuse_address = True

Server(("0.0.0.0", {GUEST_PORT}), Handler).serve_forever()
"""


async def main() -> None:
    # export BOXLITE_API_KEY=<YOUR_API_KEY> before running
    rt = Boxlite.rest(BoxliteRestOptions(
        url=os.environ.get("BOXLITE_REST_URL", "https://api.boxlite.ai"),
        credential=ApiKeyCredential(os.environ["BOXLITE_API_KEY"]),
    ))

    box_id = None
    connection = None
    try:
        box = await rt.create(
            BoxOptions(
                image=IMAGE,
                # Required for a tunnel: inbound is disabled by default,
                # and a tunnel against a private box is refused.
                network=NetworkSpec(inbound=InboundNetworkSpec(mode="enabled")),
            ),
            name=f"tunnel-bytes-{int(time.time())}",
        )
        box_id = box.id
        await box.start()

        launch = await box.exec("sh", args=[
            "-c",
            f"nohup python3 -u -c {shlex.quote(SERVER_CODE)} "
            "> /tmp/line-server.log 2>&1 & echo launched",
        ])
        await launch.wait()
        await asyncio.sleep(2)  # give the server time to bind

        tunnel = await box.network.tunnel(GUEST_PORT)
        connection = await tunnel.connect()

        await connection.write(b"ping over a raw tunnel\n")

        # Signals that you have finished sending. This server replies to the
        # newline, so it does not depend on seeing the half-close -- see Limits.
        await connection.shutdown_write()

        reply = bytearray()
        while b"\n" not in reply:
            chunk = await connection.read(4096)  # max_bytes must be non-zero
            if not chunk:  # empty read: the far side closed the stream
                break
            reply.extend(chunk)

        print(f"reply: {bytes(reply)!r}")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"byte stream demo failed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
    finally:
        if connection is not None:
            try:
                await connection.close()
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"connection close failed: {exc}")
        if box_id:
            try:
                await rt.remove(box_id, force=True)
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"remove failed: {exc}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

## Read until the far side closes

`read(max_bytes)` returns up to `max_bytes` bytes, and an **empty `bytes` object once
the far side has closed** — that empty read is the end-of-stream signal the loop above
breaks on. There is no separate EOF flag to check.

| What you do | What happens |
| - | - |
| `read(n)` with data available | Up to `n` bytes |
| `read(n)` after the far side closed | `b""` — stop reading |
| `read(0)` | `ValueError: max_bytes must be non-zero` |
| `read(n)` after your own `close()` | A BoxLite error carrying `connection is closed` |

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Not using asyncio?** `SyncBox.network` and `SyncBox.tunnel(port)` return
> `SyncNetworkHandle` and `SyncTunnelForwarder`, the synchronous equivalents of
> everything on this page.

# Use API keys without putting them in your box
Source: https://docs.boxlite.ai/cloud/secrets

Make an LLM call from a Cloud box using Python, TypeScript, or CLI without putting the model key inside the box.

Let code inside your box call an authenticated HTTPS API while keeping the credential out of its environment and configuration files. Supply the real value when you create the box; BoxLite's outbound proxy inserts it into selected request headers.

Your application uses a placeholder such as `<BOXLITE_SECRET:model>`. You choose which destination hosts and headers receive the real value.

## Make your first LLM call

Run one inference request inside a box. Your workstation supplies the real model key to BoxLite; the code inside the box sends only `<BOXLITE_SECRET:model>` and receives the model's reply.

You need an OpenAI API key with access to `gpt-4.1-mini` and a [BoxLite Cloud API key](/cloud/api-keys). Run the commands on your workstation. The examples create a disposable box, print the reply, and remove the box automatically.

Using another OpenAI-compatible provider? Change `api.openai.com` in both the Secret host and request URL, and change the model ID. Use that provider's key. The real key still belongs only in the Secret configuration.

> [tab] Python
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> python3 -m venv .venv
> source .venv/bin/activate
> python -m pip install --upgrade boxlite
> ```
>
> Save as `llm_secret.py` and paste your **BoxLite Cloud API key**, then your **OpenAI API key**, at the prompts:
>
> ```python llm_secret.py theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> import asyncio
> import json
> from getpass import getpass
>
> import boxlite
>
>
> async def main():
>     cloud_key = getpass("BoxLite Cloud API key: ")
>     runtime = boxlite.Boxlite.rest(boxlite.BoxliteRestOptions(
>         url="https://api.boxlite.ai",
>         credential=boxlite.ApiKeyCredential(cloud_key),
>     ))
>     token = getpass("OpenAI API key: ")
>     box = None
>
>     async def run(command, args):
>         execution = await box.exec(command, args=args)
>         output = "".join([part async for part in execution.stdout()])
>         result = await execution.wait()
>         if result.exit_code != 0:
>             raise RuntimeError(f"{command} failed with exit code {result.exit_code}")
>         return output
>
>     try:
>         box = await runtime.create(boxlite.BoxOptions(
>             image="python:alpine",
>             auto_stop=0,
>             auto_delete=0,
>             secrets=[boxlite.Secret(
>                 name="model",
>                 value=token,
>                 hosts=["api.openai.com"],
>                 headers={"Authorization": "Bearer {value}"},
>             )],
>         ))
>         print(f"Created box: {box.id}")
>         await box.start()
>         request = """
> import json, ssl, urllib.request
> payload = {
>     "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",
>     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one short sentence."}],
>     "max_tokens": 64,
> }
> request = urllib.request.Request(
>     "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
>     data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
>     headers={
>         "Content-Type": "application/json",
>         "Authorization": "Bearer <BOXLITE_SECRET:model>",
>     },
> )
> context = ssl.create_default_context(cafile="/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt")
> with urllib.request.urlopen(request, context=context, timeout=60) as response:
>     print(json.load(response)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
> """
>         print((await run("python", ["-c", request])).strip())
>     finally:
>         try:
>             if box is not None:
>                 await runtime.remove(box.id, force=True)
>                 print("Removed the test box")
>         finally:
>             runtime.close()
>
>
> asyncio.run(main())
>
> ```
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> python llm_secret.py
> ```

> [tab] TypeScript
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> npm install @boxlite-ai/boxlite tsx
> ```
>
> Enter your Cloud API key, then your provider key, on your workstation (Bash or Zsh):
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> read -r -s "BOXLITE_API_KEY"
> export BOXLITE_API_KEY
> read -r -s OPENAI_API_KEY
> export OPENAI_API_KEY
> ```
>
> Save as `llm_secret.ts`:
>
> ```typescript llm_secret.ts theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> import { ApiKeyCredential, BoxliteRestOptions, JsBoxlite } from '@boxlite-ai/boxlite';
>
> async function main() {
>   const cloudKey = process.env.BOXLITE_API_KEY;
>   if (!cloudKey) throw new Error('Set BOXLITE_API_KEY on your workstation');

>     return output;
>   }
>   try {
>     box = await runtime.create({ image: 'python:alpine', autoStop: 0, autoDelete: 0,
>       secrets: [{name: 'model', value: token, hosts: ['api.openai.com'],
>         headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer {value}' }}],
>     });
>     console.log(`Created box: ${box.id}`);
>     await box.start();
>     const request = `
> import json, ssl, urllib.request
> payload = {
>     "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",
>     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one short sentence."}],
>     "max_tokens": 64,
> }
> request = urllib.request.Request(
>     "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
>     data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
>     headers={
>         "Content-Type": "application/json",
>         "Authorization": "Bearer <BOXLITE_SECRET:model>",
>     },
> )
> context = ssl.create_default_context(cafile="/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt")
> with urllib.request.urlopen(request, context=context, timeout=60) as response:
>     print(json.load(response)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
> `;
>     console.log((await run("python", ["-c", request])).trim());
>   } finally {
>     try { if (box) { await runtime.remove(box.id, true); console.log('Removed the test box'); } }
>     finally { runtime.close(); }
>   }
> }
> main().catch(error => { console.error(error); process.exitCode = 1; });
>
> ```
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> npx tsx llm_secret.ts
> ```

> [tab] CLI + REST
>
> The CLI has no Secret-creation flag. This shell workflow creates the box through the REST API, then uses `boxlite exec` to run inference. Do not put the real credential in `boxlite create -e`.
>
> Install the latest CLI. You also need Bash, `curl`, and `jq` on your workstation:
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> curl -fsSL https://sh.boxlite.ai | sh
> ```
>
> Save as `llm_secret.sh`:
>
> ```bash llm_secret.sh theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> #!/usr/bin/env bash
> set -euo pipefail
> BASE='https://api.boxlite.ai'
> if [[ -z "${BOXLITE_API_KEY:-}" ]]; then
>   read -r -s -p 'BoxLite Cloud API key: ' BOXLITE_API_KEY
>   printf '\n'
> fi
> export BOXLITE_API_KEY
> WORK=$(mktemp -d)
> BOX=''
> api() {
>   local route=$1
>   shift
>   printf 'header = "Authorization: Bearer %s"\n' "$BOXLITE_API_KEY" |
>     curl -q --config - --fail --silent --show-error "$BASE/v1$route" "$@"
> }
> cleanup() {
>   if [[ -n "$BOX" ]]; then
>     if api "/boxes/$BOX?force=true" -X DELETE >/dev/null; then
>       printf 'Removed the test box\n'
>     else
>       printf 'Cleanup failed; remove box %s in the console\n' "$BOX" >&2
>     fi
>   fi
>   rm -rf "$WORK"
> }
> trap cleanup EXIT
> read -r -s -p 'OpenAI API key: ' OPENAI_API_KEY
> printf '\n'
> export OPENAI_API_KEY
> jq -n '{image:"python:alpine",auto_stop:0,auto_delete:0,
>   secrets:[{name:"model",value:env.OPENAI_API_KEY,hosts:["api.openai.com"],
>     headers:{Authorization:"Bearer {value}"}}]}' > "$WORK/create.json"
> unset OPENAI_API_KEY
> BOX=$(api /boxes -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
>   --data-binary @"$WORK/create.json" | jq -er '.box_id')
> printf 'Created box: %s\n' "$BOX"
> boxcli() { boxlite --home "$WORK/home" --url "$BASE" --path-prefix '' "$@"; }
> boxcli start "$BOX" >/dev/null
> REQUEST=$(cat <<'PY'
> import json, ssl, urllib.request
> payload = {
>     "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",
>     "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one short sentence."}],
>     "max_tokens": 64,
> }
> request = urllib.request.Request(
>     "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
>     data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
>     headers={
>         "Content-Type": "application/json",
>         "Authorization": "Bearer <BOXLITE_SECRET:model>",
>     },
> )
> context = ssl.create_default_context(cafile="/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt")
> with urllib.request.urlopen(request, context=context, timeout=60) as response:
>     print(json.load(response)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
> PY
> )
> boxcli exec "$BOX" -- python -c "$REQUEST"
>
> ```
>
> ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> bash llm_secret.sh
> ```

Expected output (the model's wording can vary):

```text theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
Created box: <BOX_ID>
Hello! How can I help you today?
Removed the test box
```

A successful authenticated model response demonstrates that the proxy injected a usable credential. The model key is supplied only to `Secret.value`; it is not passed to the guest command or guest environment.

## How it works

```mermaid theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Code inside the box
    participant Proxy as BoxLite outbound proxy
    participant API as Allowed HTTPS API
    App->>Proxy: Authorization header with a placeholder
    Note over Proxy: Match host and replace the configured header
    Proxy->>API: Authorization header with the real credential
    API-->>App: API response
```

A Secret is configured on a box through `BoxOptions.secrets`. This guide does not require a separate secret-store setup or a public tunnel.

> [!NOTE]
>
> A Secret controls where a credential is injected. It does not restrict all outbound traffic. Use [network policy](/cloud/network-policy#outbound-what-the-box-can-reach) if you also need to limit which destinations the box can reach.

## Connect your own API

Once the demo works, configure your production box with the API's real hostname, credential, and authentication header. Read the real credential on your workstation or trusted backend:

> [tab] Python
>
> ```python theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> from getpass import getpass
> import boxlite
>
> provider_secret = boxlite.Secret(
>     name="model",
>     value=getpass("Provider API key: "),
>     hosts=["api.your-provider.com"],
>     headers={"Authorization": "Bearer {value}"},
> )
> # Pass secrets=[provider_secret] to BoxOptions when creating the box.
> ```

> [tab] TypeScript
>
> ```typescript theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> // This runs on the trusted workstation or backend, outside the box.
> const providerKey = process.env.PROVIDER_API_KEY;
> if (!providerKey) throw new Error("Set PROVIDER_API_KEY on the host");
> const providerSecret = {
>   name: "model",
>   value: providerKey,
>   hosts: ["api.your-provider.com"],
>   headers: { Authorization: "Bearer {value}" },
> };
> // Pass secrets: [providerSecret] in runtime.create(...).
> ```

> [tab] CLI + REST
>
> The `POST /v1/boxes` request accepts the same configuration in JSON:
>
> ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
> {
>   "secrets": [{
>     "name": "model",
>     "value": "<YOUR_PROVIDER_KEY>",
>     "hosts": ["api.your-provider.com"],
>     "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer {value}"}
>   }]
> }
> ```
>
> Merge this field into the create request. Supply the real value from your trusted host's secret store; avoid placing it in shell history or committing it to a JSON file. The shell example keeps its request body in a restricted temporary directory and deletes it during cleanup.

Replace `api.your-provider.com` with the hostname from your API URL, without `https://` or a path. Pass `secrets=[provider_secret]` in the `BoxOptions` used to create your box.

Inside the box, configure your HTTP client or agent with the placeholder **`<BOXLITE_SECRET:model>`**, not the real key. For example, the request should contain:

```text theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
Authorization: Bearer <BOXLITE_SECRET:model>
```

If your agent requires an environment variable such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`, set that variable to the placeholder through the box environment configuration:

Python uses `env=[("OPENAI_API_KEY", "<BOXLITE_SECRET:model>")]`; TypeScript uses `env: [{ key: "OPENAI_API_KEY", value: "<BOXLITE_SECRET:model>" }]`; the REST create body uses `"env": {"OPENAI_API_KEY": "<BOXLITE_SECRET:model>"}`. Keep the Secret configuration alongside it.

Configure the agent's API base URL separately. It must use the hostname you listed in `hosts`.

Validate with a read-only endpoint on the real provider that requires authentication. Check for its expected successful response; do not print authorization headers or full debug request logs.

### Choose the authentication header

Use the header required by your API:

| API authentication | Secret `headers` | Header sent from inside the box |
| - | - | - |
| Bearer token | `{"Authorization": "Bearer {value}"}` | `Authorization: Bearer <BOXLITE_SECRET:model>` |
| API-key header | `{"X-Api-Key": "{value}"}` | `X-Api-Key: <BOXLITE_SECRET:model>` |

`{value}` is the proxy's template variable. `<BOXLITE_SECRET:model>` is the dummy value used by your application. They have different roles; keep the real credential only in `Secret.value`.

**The request must already contain the configured header.** BoxLite replaces its value when the host matches, even if the original value is empty or differs from the placeholder. It does not add a missing header. Other headers remain unchanged.

This is header injection, not a general search-and-replace operation over URLs, query strings, or request bodies. It is intended for authenticated HTTPS APIs, not credentials needed by a process locally.

## Restart, replace, or retire a credential

A box retains its Secret configuration across a stop/start. You do not need to pass the key again each time you resume it.

To adopt a new credential using the workflow in this guide, create a replacement box with the updated Secret, verify authentication, then move work to it. Changing a local Python variable does not update a box that already exists.

Remove a box when you no longer need it. Deleting the box does not revoke the credential at its provider; revoke the provider key separately when retiring it.

For agents with a public service, you can [move a fixed domain to the replacement box](/cloud/domains#move-the-service-without-changing-its-url).

## Security boundaries

* Keep real keys out of `BoxOptions.env`, images, uploaded files, agent prompts, and commands executed inside the box.
* Use the narrowest destination hosts and provider permissions your application needs. Code in the box can use the credential's authority at those hosts.
* A trusted destination receives the real credential. If it reflects the value in its response, code in the box can read that response.
* Keep TLS verification enabled. With a custom image or HTTP library, ensure it trusts the box's proxy CA through the system CA bundle.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to check |
| - | - |
| Cloud rejects the SDK request | Use your BoxLite Cloud API key for `ApiKeyCredential`; use the provider key only for `Secret.value`. |
| `Secret` reports a missing `headers` argument | Supply an explicit mapping, such as `headers={"Authorization": "Bearer {value}"}`. |
| The provider returns `401` or `403` | Check the credential, its permissions, the exact destination hostname, and whether the application sends the configured header. |
| No injection occurs | A matching host and an existing target header are both required; a placeholder in an unrelated header does not trigger injection. |
| TLS certificate verification fails | Configure your client to use the box's system CA bundle, as the Python example does. Do not disable verification. |
| A request to a different host still contains the placeholder | Expected: that host is outside the Secret's injection scope. |
| The example fails during cleanup | Use the printed box ID to remove the test box in the console after connectivity returns. |
